title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act I, Scene I — Athens. The palace of Theseus.
openingText: THESEUS: Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour draws on apace; four happy days bring in another moon: but, O, methinks, how slow this old moon wanes! She lingers my desires, like to a step-dame or a dowager long withering out a young man's revenue. HIPPOLYTA: Four days will quickly steep themselves in night; four nights will quickly dream away the time.
about:
A Midsummer Night's Dream is Shakespeare's most playful comedy. Two pairs of young Athenian lovers, a troupe of working-class actors rehearsing a play, and a court of fairies all find themselves in the woods outside Athens on a magical midsummer night. Identities get mixed up. Bottom the weaver gets a donkey's head. Titania, queen of the fairies, falls in love with him. Eventually morning comes and everyone returns to themselves changed.

Shakespeare wrote it in the mid-1590s, around the same time as Romeo and Juliet. The two plays are companions — one tragedy and one comedy of young love. The Dream is one of the most often-performed of his plays, partly because it is genuinely funny across centuries and partly because the play's argument about what love does to people is treated lightly without being shallow.

angleCards.title: Love as temporary insanity.
angleCards.text: The love potion is a metaphor for something Shakespeare thinks is already true: romantic love makes people irrational, arbitrary, and easily redirected. Notice whether the play thinks this is beautiful or absurd — or both.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as Shakespeare's study of love as a form of temporary madness — whether the Dream endorses romantic passion or gently mocks it.

angleCards.title: Shakespeare on theatre.
angleCards.text: Bottom and his friends are terrible actors who take their play completely seriously. Their performance of Pyramus and Thisbe — and the aristocrats' condescending commentary — is Shakespeare examining the relationship between performer, play, and audience.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the play-within-a-play — the mechanicals' performance — as Shakespeare commenting on theatre itself, on what audiences need from stories.

angleCards.title: Bottom's translation.
angleCards.text: He is turned into an ass and loved by the Fairy Queen — and takes both in stride with a kind of natural dignity. His waking speech about the dream he cannot describe ("I have had a most rare vision") is one of the most quietly profound moments in all Shakespeare.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Bottom's transformation — what it means to be "translated," and whether his night with Titania is the most honest moment in the whole play.

angleCards.title: Which world is more irrational?
angleCards.text: Athens has laws forcing daughters to marry men chosen by fathers or face death. The fairy world has enchantments forcing people to fall in love with donkeys. Shakespeare keeps the question open: civilisation and magic are competing versions of coercion.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to ask which world in the play is more irrational — the human world with its laws and arranged marriages, or the fairy world with its quarrels and magic.

cast.name: Puck
cast.description: Oberon's servant and the engine of most of the comedy's chaos. He applies the love potion to the wrong man, observes the consequences with delight, and asks at the end whether any of it was real.

cast.name: Oberon
cast.description: He starts the whole plot by enchanting his own wife in a spite-fuelled quarrel over a changeling boy. He is not presented as wicked — just capricious, as the powerful tend to be.

cast.name: Titania
cast.description: Bewitched into loving Bottom by her husband's petty revenge. Her scenes with Bottom are at once farcical and oddly tender. She is not diminished by the enchantment — if anything, she is the most complete character in the fairy plot.

cast.name: Bottom
cast.description: An enthusiastic amateur actor, turned into a half-donkey, loved by a fairy queen, and entirely unbothered by any of it. He is the play's most grounded character — paradoxically the most human when he is least human in appearance.

cast.name: Helena & Hermia
cast.description: Friends whose friendship nearly breaks apart when both men chase Helena instead of Hermia. Their relationship — its tenderness and its strain — is sharper and more interesting than the romance between either of them and their eventual husbands.

cast.name: Lysander & Demetrius
cast.description: They are barely distinguishable — which is precisely the point. The women love them with total conviction; the men redirect their love like weather vanes. Shakespeare seems to be making an argument about who is doing the actual work in these relationships.

whyItMatters.title: A Comedy About How Love Lies
whyItMatters.body: Each of the four lovers spends the night being made to love the wrong person by a magic flower. The play uses the device to argue something serious: that love feels like clarity from the inside but looks like enchantment from the outside. The same person can be the right one and the wrong one in a single night.

whyItMatters.title: The Mechanicals
whyItMatters.body: The working-class players who rehearse and perform "Pyramus and Thisbe" are some of Shakespeare's funniest creations. They also embody one of his deeper interests: ordinary people taking art seriously. The play does not condescend to them. They are the heart of the comedy.

whyItMatters.title: The Forest Outside the City
whyItMatters.body: The Athens of the play is rule, marriage law, and order. The forest is dream, transformation, and disorder. The play sets up a permanent geography that English literature has used ever since: the wood is where the city's order is suspended, and where the changes happen that the city cannot.
